passage:
You keep saying that boy on your phone is like a friend, Santosh. Let me tell you about my friend on the radio.
I was fifteen. Every night at nine, a woman called Sunita Kiran read letters from girls like me on the radio. She laughed at our jokes, she remembered names, she said, "My dear listeners, you are my family." I felt she was talking only to me.
One night she said she used Chandan Glow powder every day and so should I. I took my whole Diwali money to the market and bought three tins.
My face broke out. When I wrote to her, "from Minakshi, your listener", I got a printed card back. Later my cousin at the radio station told me the powder company paid for that whole half-hour.
I still liked her voice. But I stopped buying what she said.

qa.q: How many tins of powder did young Minakshi buy?
qa.a: Minakshi bought three tins with her whole Diwali money.

qa.q: Why did fifteen-year-old Minakshi trust the powder advice so easily?
qa.a: Minakshi felt that Sunita Kiran was talking only to her, like family, so she believed the advice came from a friend and did not question it.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Minakshi listened?
qa.a: Receiving only a printed card and then learning the company paid for the half-hour showed her the friendly voice was also selling.

qa.q: How might Sunita Kiran's show have looked to the powder company?
qa.a: To the company, the warm, family-like show was a way to reach girls who trusted the host, which is exactly why they paid for it.

grounding: A woman tells Santosh how at fifteen she trusted a friendly radio host like family and bought a product that turned out to be paid promotion.

It was 11:40 at night and the discount code ran out at midnight.
Vinita had watched Pari's videos every day for a year. Pari talked about exam stress and her own acne, and once she replied to Vinita's comment with a heart. So when Pari said, "Guys, this serum changed my skin, I'd never lie to you," Vinita believed her.
The serum cost 1,200 rupees, almost all the money she had kept from her birthday. The phone was at 3 percent.
Aditi, sharing the room, leaned over. "Why is there a tiny 'paid partnership' line under the name?"
Vinita hadn't seen it. She felt her face go hot, like she'd been caught out by someone she trusted.
"She still might like it," Aditi said. "But she's also paid for it."
The phone died at 11:52. Vinita decided to read some reviews in the morning.

qa.a: Aditi noticed a tiny "paid partnership" line under the name.

qa.a: Vinita felt embarrassed and a little betrayed; her face went hot, as if someone she trusted had caught her out.

qa.q: What was the turning point that slowed Vinita down?
qa.a: Aditi pointing out the paid partnership line, and then the phone dying, gave Vinita a pause to check reviews in the morning instead of buying under the midnight deadline.

Every night after homework, Kwame watched Hiroshi's gaming streams in his bedroom in Leeds. Hiroshi remembered regulars' names. Once he had read out Kwame's comment and said, "Good luck on your exam, mate." Kwame grinned for a week.
So when Hiroshi said, "Honestly, this headset changed my life, you lot need it," Kwame didn't check anything. He spent his birthday money that same evening.
The headset was fine. Just fine. His old one had been nearly as good.
A week later his cousin Ama scrolled down the video description. In small grey letters: "Paid partnership. Link earns me commission."
"He never said," Kwame muttered.
"He kind of did," Ama said. "Just not out loud."
Kwame stared at the screen. It felt like finding out a friend had been selling to him at his own birthday.

qa.q: What did the small grey letters in the description say?
qa.a: 'Paid partnership. Link earns me commission.'

qa.q: Why did Kwame buy the headset without checking anything?
qa.a: Kwame trusted Hiroshi like a friend and had felt warmly noticed when Hiroshi read out the comment, so the pitch felt like a friend's tip, not an ad.

qa.q: What could Kwame check before buying a creator's recommendation next time?
qa.a: Kwame could look in the description for 'paid' or 'commission', wait a day, and read reviews from people who are not being paid.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi see the regulars who buy through the link?
qa.a: Hiroshi may genuinely enjoy them, but each purchase also earns commission, so the friendly tone and the sales pitch are mixed together.

grounding: Shows a teenager who feels a streamer is a friend buying a recommended headset without noticing it was a paid partnership.

In the hostel common room, Shankar held up a small bottle. "Face wash. Mallika-akka uses it." Mallika-akka was the study creator whose morning-routine videos half the hostel watched; she called her followers "my little siblings".
Keerthana, the Class 12 prefect, turned the bottle over. "Did she say she was paid?"
"She wouldn't take money to lie to us. She talks to us like family."
Keerthana opened the video on her phone and paused it at the fourteenth second. A tiny tag flashed: "Collab." Then she opened the product page. The creator's discount code was right there.
Shankar sat down slowly. "So when she says 'trust me'..."
"She might mean it," Keerthana said. "She's also earning. Both can be true."
Shankar's face burned. He put the bottle on his shelf and sent a screenshot of the tag to his friends' group.

qa.q: What tag flashed when Keerthana paused the video?
qa.a: A tiny tag flashed: 'Collab.'

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when he saw the tag, and why?
qa.a: Shankar felt embarrassed, his face burning, because he had trusted Mallika-akka like family and had not noticed she was being paid.

qa.q: What steps did Keerthana show that Shankar can use again?
qa.a: Pausing to look for a paid tag, checking whether the product page carries the creator's code, and remembering that warmth and earning can both be true.

qa.q: What would change if Mallika-akka had said out loud that the video was paid?
qa.a: Shankar and the others could have weighed the face wash as an advertisement from the start instead of treating it like family advice.

grounding: Shows a teenager trusting a friendly creator like family and buying her product without noticing the paid collaboration tag.

Yesterday my brother showed me that your planner post had a "sponsored" line in the description, further down than I'd ever scrolled.
I'm not angry exactly. I'm confused. Were the 4 am videos real too?
I still like your videos. But from now on I'll read descriptions before I buy anything, and ask Ammi first.
Shalini
